title: Forklift Safety Refresher: Inspect, Yield, Stay Stable
description: A 24-minute, scenario-based refresher for about 220 forklift operators across three distribution centers (a fictional client). It targets pedestrian conflicts at intersections and dock doors, tip-overs from carrying raised loads through turns, and pre-shift inspections that get signed without being done. Operators make the calls themselves: they inspect a truck, choose how to approach a blind intersection or a busy dock door, and decide how to carry a load through a turn.

sections.title: Why We're Here: Your Floor, Your Numbers

blocks.text:
Forklift Safety Refresher: Inspect, Yield, Stay Stable

Last year's near misses: mostly pedestrians at intersections and dock doors, plus a couple of raised-load turns.
Also: pre-shift checks sometimes signed, not done.

About 24 minutes. Your place is saved.

You're certified, and many of you have run trucks on these floors for years, so this isn't a rules lecture. It's about the quick calls you make on a busy shift. Last year, most near misses across our three DCs were pedestrian conflicts at intersections and dock doors, plus a couple of tip-over scares from turning with a raised load. And pre-shift checks sometimes get signed without being done. Over the next 24 minutes, you'll make those calls yourself.

pages.title: Quick Poll: What Do You See Most?

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Clean layout with a muted photo of a DC floor behind a semi-opaque panel. Standard radio-button options.

blocks.text:
Quick question, not scored.
Which of these do you see most on your shift?

( ) People stepping out at intersections or dock doors
( ) Loads carried raised through turns
( ) Checklists signed without a real check
( ) Honestly, none of these
Before we start, one quick question, not scored. Which of these do you see most often on your shift?

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Course menu with four large tiles. Each tile has a realistic photo thumbnail (truck inspection, intersection, raised load, operator at a terminal), a live-text title and the duration. Tile states: Available (no icon), Locked (padlock icon plus the word 'Locked'), Done (check icon plus the word 'Done'). Tile 4 has two extra states: Passed (check icon plus the word 'Passed') and Attempts used (information icon plus the words 'Attempts used').

blocks.text:
Your route:
1. The Pre-Shift Inspection That Actually Counts (6 min)
2. Intersections and Dock Doors: Seeing People First (6 min)
3. Loads, Turns and Tip-Overs (6 min)
4. Final Check (about 5 min)

Stopping early? Your place is saved.

Three parts of about six minutes each, then a short final check. They open in order the first time through. If your huddle runs short, close the course; it picks up where you left off. Let's start where every shift starts: with the truck.

sections.title: The Pre-Shift Inspection That Actually Counts

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Photo or short video: Marcus (40s to 50s, hi-vis vest, safety footwear) climbing into a counterbalance truck numbered 07 in the truck parking or charging area, clipboard and checklist on the seat. Dock doors with three trailers in the background. '5:50 a.m.' appears as live text, top left.

blocks.text:
5:50 a.m. Truck 07.
Marcus Reyes: 14 years on counterbalance trucks.
Three trailers already on the doors.

Ten to six. Marcus Reyes has run counterbalance trucks for fourteen years. Truck 07 was fine yesterday, and the day before. Three trailers are on the doors, and Priya, his supervisor, wants the first one unloaded by six thirty. Marcus could tick every box in a minute without leaving the seat. Most days, nothing would happen. So what does that minute miss?

blocks.alt: Two side-by-side pictures of workers in a warehouse.
blocks.description: Worked-example video or animated photo sequence (about 40 seconds), split screen. LEFT, live-text label 'One-minute check': Marcus seated, glancing at the display, ticking boxes, signing. RIGHT, live-text label 'Real check': Marcus walking around truck 07; close-ups of (1) left fork heel wear with a fine crack, (2) fluid drips and a wet patch under the mast, (3) Marcus selecting reverse with no alarm. Each defect is marked as the narration names it by a double-stroke outline (white inner line, dark outer line) with a numbered live-text label, so the marker reaches at least 3:1 contrast on ligh...

blocks.text:
Same truck. Two checks.
Look, touch, test.

One-minute check: 0 defects found
Real check: 3 defects found

Most defects don't show from the seat. Here's truck 07, checked two ways. On the left, the one-minute version: glance at the gauges, tick, sign. Every box says OK. On the right, the same truck, checked on foot. Wear at the heel of the left fork, with a fine crack starting. Hydraulic fluid under the mast. Then the tests: horn fine, reverse alarm silent. Each one takes away a margin you rely on: fork strength, lift control, and the warning people listen for.

pages.title: Easy to Skip, Expensive to Miss

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of a counterbalance truck with numbered marker shapes (double stroke, global note 5) on each area, matching the numbered buttons. Each reveal layer shows a close-up photo of that item plus live text. The 'Reach truck extras' layer shows a reach truck close-up (baselegs, load wheels, operator presence pedal).

blocks.text:
Easy to skip. Expensive to miss.
Select any item to see why it matters.
These are the items that get skipped most. Know them cold? Move on. Newer? Select a few to see why each one is on your checklist.

items.title: Forks
items.text: Look for cracks, bends and heel wear, and check the locking pins. A worn heel can fail under a load you've lifted a hundred times.

items.title: Chains
items.text: Check for stretch, kinks, rust and uneven tension. If a chain fails, the carriage drops, along with whatever is on it.

items.title: Hydraulics
items.text: Look for leaks at hoses, fittings and cylinders, and for fluid under the mast. A leak can mean a load that drifts down or a lift that fails.

items.title: Tires
items.text: Check for chunks, cuts, flat spots and wear (and pressure on pneumatic tires). Damaged tires reduce stability, especially in turns.

items.title: Horn, lights, reverse or travel alarm
items.text: Test them, don't assume. The horn, the lights and the reverse alarm (counterbalance) or travel alarm (reach truck) are how pedestrians know you're there.

items.title: Brakes
items.text: Test the service and parking brakes before you lift anything. You need them most when you're loaded.

items.title: Seatbelt or restraint
items.text: Check that it latches and isn't cut or frayed. On a sit-down truck, it keeps you inside the overhead guard in a tip-over.

items.title: Data plate
items.text: It must be present and readable. It's how you know the rated capacity and load center.

items.title: Battery or LPG
items.text: 'Electric: cables and connectors undamaged, no corrosion. LPG: cylinder secure, connection tight, no smell of gas.'

items.title: Reach truck extras
items.text: 'Also check the reach mechanism, the load wheels in the baselegs, and the operator presence pedal.'

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Two large photo buttons: a sit-down counterbalance truck and a reach truck matching the fleet model, each with a live-text label.

blocks.text:
Your turn. Inspect a truck.
Which do you run most?
Your turn. Pick the truck you run most, inspect it item by item, and select Done when you'd sign. It isn't timed.

blocks.description: High-resolution photo or 3D render of a sit-down counterbalance truck (LPG or electric to match the fleet [CLIENT TO CONFIRM]), three-quarter view. 8 inspectable items in walk-around order: 4 planted defects (1 left fork heel wear with a hairline crack; 3 fluid weeping at the lift cylinder hose fitting with a wet patch under the mast; 5 seatbelt buckle that won't latch; 7 silent reverse alarm) and 4 normal items with harmless cosmetic wear so the learner has to judge (2 chains with surface grime; 4 tires with light sidewall scuffing; 6 LPG cylinder with dust; 8 brakes). Operational tests sit o...

blocks.prompt: Truck 07, walk-around and tests. Which of these would you flag as a defect?

options.text: Left fork heel worn, with a hairline crack starting
Lift chains with surface grime
Fluid weeping at the lift cylinder hose fitting, wet patch under the mast
Light scuffing on the tire sidewalls
Seatbelt buckle won't latch
Dust on the LPG cylinder
Reverse alarm silent when you back up

blocks.feedback_correct: Right: four real defects. The fork crack, the leak, the belt and the alarm each take away a margin you rely on. Grime, scuffs and dust are cosmetic.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The four defects are the fork heel crack, the leak at the hose fitting, the seatbelt buckle and the silent reverse alarm. Grime, scuffs and dust are cosmetic. Try again.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard, a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift and a worker in a hi-vis vest walking in a warehouse aisle. A warning sign marks the hazard.
blocks.description: High-resolution photo or 3D render of a reach truck matching the fleet [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: model, operator stance and entry position]. 8 inspectable items in walk-around order: 4 planted defects (2 kinked, rust-stiffened link near the top of the left lift chain; 4 cracked battery connector housing with copper showing on one cable; 6 silent horn; 7 truck creeps on the travel control with the operator presence pedal released, shown as a short clip) and 4 normal items with harmless cosmetic wear (1 forks with scuffed paint; 3 reach mechanism and hoses; 5 data plate with edge scratches but readabl...

blocks.prompt: Reach truck R12. Which of these would you flag as a defect?

options.text: Scuffed paint on the forks
A kinked, rust-stiffened link near the top of the left lift chain
Reach mechanism and hoses clean and dry
Cracked battery connector housing, copper showing on one cable
Data plate with edge scratches, every value readable
Horn silent when pressed
Truck creeps on the travel control with the presence pedal released

blocks.feedback_correct: Right: the chain, the battery connector, the horn and the creeping travel control are all defects.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The defects are the kinked chain link, the cracked battery connector, the silent horn and the creeping travel control. Paint scuffs and edge scratches are cosmetic. Try again.

blocks.alt: An icon of a check.
blocks.description: Three-column decision graphic in live text, each column marked by a different shape icon plus a label: a check mark ('Operate'), a clipboard ('Operate and report'), a tag ('Tag out'). Under the Tag out column, a photo of the client's out-of-service tag [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: tag design]. Sources line in smaller text at the bottom (still at least 4.5:1 contrast).

blocks.text:
Every check ends one of three ways:
- Passes: operate.
- Minor, no safety impact: operate and report.
- Affects safe operation: tag out, report, don't operate.
Not sure? Tag it out and ask.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: examine before use, at least daily.

Every check ends one of three ways. Everything passes: you operate. Something minor that doesn't affect safe operation, like a torn seat cover: operate and report it. Anything that affects how the truck lifts, steers, stops, warns people or protects you: tag it, report it to your shift supervisor, and don't drive it. OSHA requires that check before use, at least daily, and an unsafe truck stays out of service until it's repaired.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift at the loading dock. A warning sign marks the hazard.
blocks.description: Close-up of the cracked fork heel (same asset as M1-S03), with a handheld radio clipped to the operator's vest in the foreground and the dock with a waiting trailer blurred in the background.

blocks.prompt:
You're on truck 07 and your check finds a crack at the heel of the left fork.
The first trailer has waited 10 minutes. Priya's on the radio.
What do you do?

options.text: Operate, but keep loads light until maintenance can look at it.
options.feedback: You run light pallets for an hour. On the fourth, the fork tip catches the pallet deck and the cracked heel gives way. The load drops at the dock edge, a few feet from Luis. Nobody's hurt this time. A cracked fork isn't a defect you can drive carefully around. Try again.

options.text: Unload the first trailer, then tag it out and report it.
options.feedback: You clear the trailer in 25 minutes, lifting every pallet on a cracked fork. Nothing breaks this time, but every lift was a gamble, and the tag came too late to protect anyone, including you. A tag-out defect comes out of service when you find it, not when it's convenient. Try again.

options.text: Tag it out now, report it and take another truck.
options.feedback: Right call. You tag truck 07 out of service (red tag on the steering wheel, key to your supervisor), report it to your shift supervisor, and take truck 09. You're eight minutes behind. Eight minutes is a lot cheaper than a dropped load.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Close-up photo of a sit-down truck seat with the cover torn along one edge, foam showing, seat firmly mounted and the seatbelt latched across it. Truck number 09 repeated in live text.

blocks.prompt:
You take truck 09. Everything passes except the seat cover, which is torn along one edge. The seat is secure and the belt latches.
What do you do?

options.text: Tag it out too. Better safe than sorry.
options.feedback: Careful, but not needed here. A torn cover doesn't affect how the truck lifts, steers, stops, warns people or protects you, so it's operate and report. Tagging out safe trucks takes them off the floor and makes real tags mean less. If you're ever genuinely unsure, tagging it out and asking is still the right call. Try again.

options.text: Operate it, and report the torn cover.
options.feedback: Right call. It doesn't affect safe operation, so you run the truck and report the cover on your checklist so it gets fixed before it turns into something bigger.

options.text: Operate it. A cover isn't worth writing up.
options.feedback: Reporting minor defects is how they get fixed before they become bigger ones, and it keeps the checklist honest. Operate, and report it. Try again.

pages.title: 'Skip It, I Drove It Last Night'

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo: Ray (night-shift operator, hi-vis vest, coffee in hand, friendly and tired) talking to the learner-operator, who stands beside a counterbalance truck holding a checklist. Neutral, collegial body language.

blocks.prompt:
6:05 a.m., another morning.
Ray (night shift): 'Line's backed up. Skip the walk-around, it was fine last night. I drove it.'

options.text: 'Fair enough.' Sign the checklist and go.
options.feedback: Ray drove it, but he wasn't checking it, and a lot can change between shifts. A fork gets clipped, a hose starts weeping overnight. When you sign the checklist, you're the one saying the truck is safe. Try again.

options.text: Do the operational tests from the seat and skip the walk-around.
options.feedback: That's half a check. The walk-around is where you find forks, chains, tires and leaks. Try again.

options.text: Do the full check, and tell Ray you'll be on the line as soon as it's done.
options.feedback: Right call. A real check takes a few minutes, and you're the one signing for this truck and driving it. If line pressure keeps squeezing out check time, raise it with Priya.

pages.title: Inspection: What to Take Back to the Floor

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard, a worker in a hi-vis vest walking and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of Marcus walking around truck 07 with the checklist. The takeaways as live text in a clean panel.

blocks.text:
Pre-shift check:
- Look, touch, test. Not from the seat.
- Your signature means you checked.
- Affects safe operation? Tag out, report, take another truck.
- Minor? Operate and report.
Get off the seat and check for real. If something affects safe operation, the truck comes out of service, however backed up the line is. Next: intersections and dock doors.

sections.title: Intersections and Dock Doors: Seeing People First

blocks.alt: Two side-by-side pictures of workers in a warehouse.
blocks.description: Split image: LEFT, Tasha's view from a reach truck, with the tall carton load blocking part of her forward view and the end cap ahead. RIGHT, Luis stepping out of a dock office door looking down at a handheld scanner. Below, a simple top-down plan (realistic diagram style, not cartoon) showing both converging on the end cap. All plan labels ('Tasha, reach truck', 'Luis', 'End cap', 'Dock office') are live Storyline text placed over the diagram, not part of the graphic.

blocks.text:
2:40 p.m. Aisle 14 meets the dock staging lane.
Tasha Greene: reach truck, 8 months in.
Luis Ortega: dock lead, on foot.

Two forty in the afternoon. Tasha Greene, eight months on reach trucks, is heading out of aisle 14 with a tall stack of cartons. Luis Ortega, the dock lead, steps out of the dock office, eyes on his scanner. A racking end cap sits between them. Neither can see the other, and each assumes the other will stop.

blocks.alt: Two side-by-side pictures of workers in a warehouse.
blocks.description: Two top-down diagrams side by side: a counterbalance truck and a reach truck (drawn to match the confirmed fleet model and operator position [CLIENT TO CONFIRM]). Blind-spot zones shown as hatched areas with live-text labels: 'Mast and load', 'Counterweight', and on the reach truck 'Operator position' [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: wording once stance is confirmed]. Hatching plus labels, never color alone.

blocks.text:
Where you can't see:
- Racking end caps and aisle ends
- Dock doors and trailer edges
- Staging lanes full of pallets
- Your truck's own blind spots

Load blocks your view? Travel with the load trailing.

Conflicts happen where views are blocked: aisle ends, end caps, dock doors, full staging lanes. Your truck adds its own blind spots. On a counterbalance, the mast and load block much of the view ahead, and the counterweight hides what's low behind you. On a reach truck, the mast, the load and where you stand each cut off part of the view. If the load blocks your view ahead, travel with it trailing.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Realistic photo or 3D still of the aisle 14 intersection from the reach truck's approach. It contains: (H1) a racking end cap on the left hiding the cross aisle; (H2) the dock office personnel door on the right opening onto the travel lane; (H3) a tall pallet stack in the staging lane blocking the view to the right; (H4) the zone directly ahead of the truck's tall load. Distractor: (D1) a convex mirror on a column.

blocks.text:
Find the conflict points.
Select every spot where a person and a truck could meet without seeing each other.
Here's the end of aisle 14 from Tasha's side. Find every spot where a person and a truck could meet without seeing each other, then select Done.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest, a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift and a visitor in an orange vest on the phone at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Realistic photo or 3D still of dock door 6 with an open trailer (door number repeated in live text). Contains: (H1) a truck driver (visitor vest) stepping off the trailer edge beside the door into the travel lane; (H2) a dark trailer interior with a worker partly visible inside; (H3) a congested staging lane with a dock worker hand-stacking between pallets. Distractors: (D1) trailer restraint engaged with its indicator showing; (D2) dock light on and aimed into the trailer.

blocks.text:
Now the dock.
Select every spot where a person and a truck could meet without seeing each other.
Now dock door 6, mid-unload. Same task.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest, a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift and a worker in a hi-vis vest on the phone in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Worked-example video (about 35 seconds) from the operator's seat, approaching the aisle 14 intersection and doing each step correctly. As the narration names each step, its number and label in a live-text sidebar list gain a bold border plus an arrow icon. Ends with a pedestrian nodding and the truck proceeding.

blocks.text:
Every intersection. Every dock door.
1. Slow down
2. Sound the horn
3. Look both ways
4. Yield to pedestrians
5. Make eye contact
6. Proceed

No eye contact? Stop and wait.

You know this one. Run all of it, every time. Slow down before the intersection, not in it. Sound the horn: OSHA requires it at cross aisles and wherever your view is blocked. Look both ways. Yield to pedestrians: at our sites, pedestrians have the right of way. Then get eye contact. The horn tells people you're there. Eye contact tells you they know. No eye contact? Stop and wait. Then proceed.

pages.title: Your Call 1: Load Blocking Your View

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's-seat photo with a tall stack of totes on the forks filling most of the forward view, and the aisle 9 end cap barely visible. Swap the photo by TruckType (counterbalance or reach truck view) if budget allows; otherwise use a counterbalance view.

blocks.prompt:
Busy afternoon. You're carrying a double stack of totes toward the aisle 9 intersection. The load blocks your view ahead.
How do you approach?

options.text: Travel forward and lean out to see around the load.
options.feedback: Leaning out puts your head and shoulders outside the overhead guard, and you still can't see properly. When the load blocks your view ahead, travel with the load trailing. Try again.

options.text: Travel with the load trailing, looking the way you're going.
options.feedback: Right. Load trailing, looking the way you're traveling. Now you can see what's ahead.

options.text: Travel forward slowly, sounding the horn the whole way.
options.feedback: The horn helps people hear you, but you still can't see them. Someone stepping out of the staging lane would be in front of your load before you knew they were there. Travel with the load trailing. Try again.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's view (load trailing) approaching the aisle 9 end cap, with a floor-marked stop line visible [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: floor markings].

blocks.prompt:
You're about 15 feet from the intersection.
What's your sequence?

options.text: Sound the horn, keep your speed, look, go through.
options.feedback: The horn's right, but at full speed you've got almost no time to react to what you see when you look. Slow down first, then the rest of the sequence. Try again.

options.text: Slow down, sound the horn, look both ways, yield, make eye contact, proceed.
options.feedback: Right. That's the full sequence. You slow down, sound the horn and start to look.

options.text: Slow down, look, go through if no one's there. Horn only if you see someone.
options.feedback: The horn isn't for the people you can see. It's for the ones you can't, behind the end cap or the pallet stack. Sound it every time. Try again.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a colleague pointing and a colleague in an office.
blocks.description: Operator's-view still: Luis about 10 feet ahead, half out from behind the end cap, head down over his scanner.

blocks.prompt: You start through. Luis steps out from behind the end cap, reading his scanner. He hasn't seen you.

options.text: Sound the horn again and keep rolling slowly. He'll step back.
options.feedback: He heard a horn, but hearing isn't seeing. The safe response is to stop, sound the horn, wait until he has seen you and is clear, then proceed. Let's look at that moment from Luis's side.

options.text: Stop. Sound the horn, wait until he's seen you and is clear, then proceed.
options.feedback: Right call. You stop, he looks up, you get a nod, he steps clear. Three seconds. Now look at the other version from his side.

options.text: Steer around him so you keep moving.
options.feedback: Startled people move unpredictably, often into the space you're steering for. The safe response is to stop, sound the horn, wait until he has seen you and is clear, then proceed. Let's see it from Luis's side.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest, a worker in a hi-vis vest on the phone and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Short POV video (about 20 seconds) from Luis's eye level: scanner screen in hand, a horn in the background, he looks up to see forks and a load emerging from behind the end cap, and the truck stops about six feet away. No contact, no injury, nothing shocking. Ends on a freeze frame of Luis stepping back.

blocks.text:
From the pedestrian's side.

A horn means 'a truck is somewhere.'
It doesn't mean 'they've seen me.'

Same moment, from Luis's side, when the operator trusts the horn. Luis hears horns all day. He's checking a pick count. When he looks up, the forks are six feet away. Two people, each sure the other had it handled.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest, a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift and a visitor in an orange vest on the phone at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Photo: a truck driver in a visitor vest stepping off the trailer edge at door 4 into the travel lane, seen from a truck about 20 feet away.

blocks.prompt:
A truck driver steps off his trailer at door 4, right into your lane.
Who has the right of way, and what's your move?

options.text: You do. Sound the horn so he steps back.
He does, but you can pass behind him if there's room.
He does. Stop, make eye contact, let him clear your path, then proceed.

blocks.feedback_correct: Correct. Pedestrians have the right of way. Stop, get eye contact, and let him clear your path before you move.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The correct answer is C: he has the right of way. Passing behind him or hoping the horn moves him depends on him staying where you expect, and drivers don't know your floor. Stop, get eye contact, let him clear, then proceed.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Photo: view from the dock edge into a dim trailer interior, with a silhouette of a worker partly visible behind stacked cartons.

blocks.prompt:
You're about to enter the trailer at door 7. It's dark inside, and you can hear someone moving.
What do you do?

options.text: Stop at the dock edge and sound the horn. Don't enter until you know where they are, they know you're coming, and the trailer is secured.
Enter slowly with your lights on. They'll hear the truck.
Enter, then sound the horn once you're inside.

blocks.feedback_correct: Correct. In a dark trailer, neither of you can see the other. Stop outside, sound the horn, and confirm where they are before you go in. Only enter a trailer that's secured with the restraint or chocks on and the dock plate in place.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The correct answer is A. Lights and engine noise don't tell you where the person is, and once you're inside there's no room to stop safely. Stop at the dock edge, sound the horn, confirm where they are and that the trailer is secured, then enter.

pages.title: Intersections and Docks: What to Take Back

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest holding a clipboard, a worker in a hi-vis vest walking and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of the aisle 14 intersection with Tasha's truck stopped and Luis giving a nod. Site controls shown as small photos with live-text labels if they exist (walkway markings, mirror, blue spot light) [CLIENT TO CONFIRM].

blocks.text:
Intersections and dock doors:
- View blocked? Load trailing, slow down, horn.
- Slow, horn, look, yield, eye contact, proceed.
- No eye contact? Stop and wait.

Our site controls: marked walkways and mirrors.

If you can't see past the load, turn it around. Run the full sequence even when the aisle looks empty. A horn only says you're near, so without eye contact, you wait. Our site controls, marked walkways and mirrors, back you up. They don't replace the sequence.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Realistic 3D reconstruction or staged video (about 25 seconds): Andre removes a pallet from the second beam level, travels with the load at chest height, turns at the aisle end, the truck leans and one wheel lifts. Freeze frame at the wheel lift, then the truck settles. No impact, no injury shown.

blocks.text:
4:50 p.m. Last pallet of the shift.
Andre Cole: 9 years on counterbalance trucks.

Ten to five. Andre Cole, nine years on counterbalance trucks, pulls his last pallet off the second beam and heads for the aisle end, load still at chest height. He turns without much braking. The truck leans hard. One wheel lifts, and for half a second it could go either way. It comes back down. Here's why.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle. A warning sign marks the hazard.
blocks.description: Animated diagram, synced to the narration: top-down truck outline with the stability triangle drawn as a bold dashed outline, and the combined center of gravity as a circle marker with the live-text label 'CG'. A side view shows the CG rising as the load rises. In the turn, the CG marker slides toward the triangle edge, with an arrow and live-text label 'Turn'. When it crosses, the edge outline thickens and the live-text label 'Outside: tip-over' appears. Plain-language labels only, no formulas, no text baked into the animation.

blocks.text:
The stability triangle:
- Three points: two front wheels and the steer axle pivot
- Truck + load = one combined center of gravity
- Inside the triangle: upright
- Higher load, faster, tighter turn: closer to the edge

Most counterbalance trucks rest on three points: the two front wheels and the pivot in the middle of the steer axle. That's the stability triangle. Truck and load share one combined center of gravity, and while it stays inside the triangle, you stay upright. Raise the load and that point climbs, so it takes less to push it sideways. A turn pushes it out; speed and rough floor push harder. Past the edge, the truck goes over. Reach trucks have a different base, but the rule is the same.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle. A warning sign marks the hazard.
blocks.description: Same top-down triangle diagram as M3-S02, with the CG marker moving to one of three positions: center (Stable), near the edge (Reduced margin) or outside (Tip-over). A side-view truck shows the load at the selected height. Three rows of segmented buttons for the settings. The result panel sits directly beneath the settings on the base slide: a headline with an icon per state (circle = Stable, triangle with exclamation mark = Reduced margin, crossed circle = Tip-over) and up to two factor lines below it, all live text.

blocks.text: Three things move the center of gravity toward the edge of the stability triangle. Open each one to see what it does.

items.title: Load height
items.text: The higher the load, the higher the combined center of gravity, and the less sideways force it takes to push it past the edge. Travel at floor height.

items.title: Speed
items.text: Speed in a turn pushes the center of gravity sideways. Braking hard in the turn throws it forward at the same time. Get your speed off on the straight.

items.title: Turn
items.text: A tight turn pushes harder than a wide, smooth one. Put all three together, a raised load, speed held and a tight turn, and the center of gravity is outside the triangle.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Short real video or 3D clip (about 30 seconds) of correct carrying: forks low and tilted back, the operator stopping to lower before traveling, braking on the straight, a smooth turn. Reach truck clip showing the travel position [CLIENT TO CONFIRM]. Then a GENERIC DATA PLATE built in Storyline as a shape group: field labels and values are live text, for example 'Rated capacity: [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: example value from a fleet data plate]' and 'Load center: [CLIENT TO CONFIRM: example value]', with both fields outlined (double stroke). No photo of real plate text.

blocks.text:
Carry it right:
- Forks low, tilted back (about 15 cm, 6 in, off the floor)
- Raise and lower only when stopped
- Slow down before the turn, not in it
- Load within data plate capacity and load center

Reach truck: mast retracted, load at travel height

So here's how to carry it. Forks low and tilted back, load against the backrest, at our SOP travel height. Raise and lower only when stopped. Get your speed off on the straight, then take the turn without more braking. Check the data plate: the capacity at the load center you're actually carrying. On a reach truck, travel with the mast retracted and the load at travel height.

blocks.alt: Two side-by-side pictures of colleagues at work.
blocks.description: Worked-example split replay, about 20 seconds: the M3-S01 footage with the stability triangle overlay from M3-S02. LEFT, live-text label 'What happened': the CG marker climbs and slides to the edge, with numbered live-text callouts. RIGHT, live-text label 'What would have prevented it': the alternate version, with the CG marker staying central and matching callouts.

blocks.text:
Andre's turn, replayed.

What led to it: load raised, speed held, late braking, tight turn.

What would have prevented it: lower at the rack, slow on the straight, wide smooth turn.

Andre's turn again, with the diagram on. Load high, speed held, late braking, tight turn: the marker slides to the edge. Now the other version: lowered at the rack, slowed on the straight, a wide, smooth turn. About four seconds slower, and the marker never gets near the edge.

pages.title: Your Call 1: The Pallet's Still Up

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's-view photo: forks raised at the third beam level with a pallet just picked, aisle stretching ahead to a visible aisle end. Small stability triangle inset showing the current CG position (high, at center).

blocks.prompt:
Aisle 22. You've just picked a pallet from the third beam level. It's still up at beam height. The aisle end is 40 feet away, then a left turn.
What do you do first?

options.text: Back out and lower as you go, to save time.
options.feedback: Lowering while you travel means two things are changing at once. As you back out, a wheel drops into a floor joint and the raised load sways. You stop it in time, but the pallet has shifted on the forks. Stop first, then lower. Try again.

options.text: Back out just enough to clear the rack, stop, lower to travel height, tilt back, then travel.
options.feedback: Right. It costs a few seconds and puts the center of gravity back where it belongs.

options.text: Leave it up. You're setting it down at the dock anyway.
options.feedback: With the load at third-beam height, the center of gravity is about as high as it gets. Forty feet and one left turn later, the marker is outside the triangle. That's how Andre's scare started. Lower before you travel. Try again.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's view approaching the aisle 22 end with the load low, and a busy main travel lane visible ahead. Stability triangle inset.

blocks.prompt:
Load's low and tilted back. The aisle end is coming up and the main lane is busy.
How do you take the turn?

options.text: Hold your speed and brake hard at the corner.
options.feedback: Braking hard at the corner throws the load forward just as the turn pushes it sideways. The marker slides to the edge. Get your speed off while you're still going straight. Try again.

options.text: Brake on the straight, enter slowly, steer smoothly, and run the intersection sequence.
options.feedback: Right call. Speed off on the straight, a smooth turn, and the intersection sequence. The pallet gets to door 3 about five seconds later than it would have. Nobody notices.

options.text: Swing wide at the same speed so the turn is gentler.
options.feedback: A wider turn helps, but speed matters most. At that speed the turn still pushes the center of gravity hard toward the edge, and you're swinging into a busy lane you haven't checked. Try again.

blocks.alt: Two side-by-side pictures of workers in a warehouse.
blocks.description: Two-panel 3D render. LEFT: operator in a sit-down counterbalance truck, belted, gripping the wheel, feet braced, leaning away from the direction of tip (arrow with live-text label 'Lean away'). RIGHT: reach truck operator showing the confirmed response, rendered on the confirmed fleet model with its confirmed stance and entry position [CLIENT TO CONFIRM; render only after Dana approves]. FALLBACK RIGHT PANEL: a photo of a reach truck operator's manual and the site SOP binder on a supervisor's desk, with the fallback text as live text. No crash or injury shown.

blocks.text:
If it starts to tip:

Sit-down counterbalance:
- Don't jump
- Stay in the seat, belt on
- Grip the wheel, brace your feet
- Lean away from the fall

Reach truck: follow the tip-over response in your SOP and your truck's operator's manual.

Everything so far is about never getting here. If a truck starts to tip, you have about a second, and instinct usually says jump. On a sit-down counterbalance, don't. Stay in the seat with your belt on, grip the wheel, brace your feet and lean away from the fall. Inside the overhead guard is the safest place to be, and operators who jump are often caught by it. On a reach truck, the right response depends on the truck's design, so follow the response in your SOP and your truck's operator's manual. Your supervisor will go through it with you.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Still: operator's-seat view of a counterbalance truck mid-turn, tilted slightly to the right. Non-graphic.

blocks.prompt:
You're on a sit-down counterbalance truck, belted in. In a turn, the truck starts to tip to the right.
What do you do?

options.text: Jump clear to the left, away from the truck.
Stay in the seat, grip the wheel, brace your feet and lean left, away from the fall.
Lean right, into the fall, to push it back down.
Unbuckle so you can get out fast once it stops.

blocks.feedback_correct: Correct. Belted in, gripping the wheel, feet braced, leaning away from the fall: that keeps you inside the overhead guard, the safest place to be.

pages.title: Loads and Turns: What to Take Back

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of a counterbalance truck carrying a pallet low and tilted back through a smooth turn, with a small stability triangle icon showing the CG centered.

blocks.text:
Loads, turns, tip-overs:
- Low and tilted back. Raise and lower only when stopped.
- Slow down before the turn.
- Know your load and your data plate.
- Know the tip-over response for your truck.

Height is the multiplier: the higher the load, the less it takes to tip you. Lower first, scrub off speed while you're still straight, and know your truck's tip-over response before you ever need it. Next, the final check.

sections.title: Final Check: Your Shift, Your Calls

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of an operator at the start of a shift, looking down a clear aisle. Rules as a live-text list.

blocks.text:
Final check:
- 10 situations from the floor
- Pass: 8 of 10 (80%)
- Reasons shown after you submit
- No timer
Last part: ten situations, and you make the call. Eight of ten to pass. Reasons come after you submit, and there's no timer.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of counterbalance truck 11 with small inset close-ups for each finding, with live-text letters beside each inset.

blocks.prompt: Pre-shift check, counterbalance truck 11. Select every finding that affects safe operation.

options.text: Hydraulic fluid dripping from a hose fitting on the mast
Seatbelt webbing cut halfway through near the buckle
Scuffed paint on the counterweight
A kinked, rust-stiffened link in a lift chain
Seat cushion cover worn at the edge

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is A, B and D. A hydraulic leak can mean a drifting load or a failed lift, a cut belt may not hold in a tip-over, and a kinked chain can fail under load. Scuffed paint and a worn seat cover don't affect safe operation; handle them as minor items under the SOP.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is A, B and D. A hydraulic leak can mean a drifting load or a failed lift, a cut belt may not hold in a tip-over, and a kinked chain can fail under load. Scuffed paint and a worn seat cover don't affect safe operation; handle them as minor items under the SOP.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Four small photo tiles, one per truck finding, each with the truck number as live text: torn seat cover, unlatched seatbelt buckle, scuffed counterweight paint, faded but readable data plate.

blocks.prompt: Four trucks, four findings from this morning's checks. Which truck must be tagged out of service before anyone drives it?

options.text: Truck 12: seat cover torn along one edge, seat secure
Truck 14: seatbelt buckle won't latch
Truck 16: scuffed paint on the counterweight
Truck 18: data plate faded, every value readable

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is truck 14. On a sit-down truck, the belt keeps you inside the overhead guard in a tip-over, so a buckle that won't latch affects safe operation: tag the truck out, report it to your shift supervisor and use another truck. The torn cover, scuffed paint and faded but readable plate don't affect safe operation, so those trucks are operate and report.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is truck 14. On a sit-down truck, the belt keeps you inside the overhead guard in a tip-over, so a buckle that won't latch affects safe operation: tag the truck out, report it to your shift supervisor and use another truck. The torn cover, scuffed paint and faded but readable plate don't affect safe operation, so those trucks are operate and report.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of a counterbalance truck parked in an aisle, forks lowered, operator stepping off.

blocks.prompt: Mid-shift, your brakes start to feel soft and the truck takes longer to stop. Your shift ends in 40 minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Finish the last 40 minutes at low speed, then tag it out and report it
Stop using it now, park it safely, tag it out and report it
Report it now and keep working until maintenance swaps the truck
Tag it out at shift end and warn the next operator

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: stop using it now, park it safely, tag it out and report it. A defect that affects stopping takes the truck out of service the moment you find it. Finishing the shift first, waiting for maintenance, or passing a warning to the next operator all mean driving on brakes you can't trust.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: stop using it now, park it safely, tag it out and report it. A defect that affects stopping takes the truck out of service the moment you find it. Finishing the shift first, waiting for maintenance, or passing a warning to the next operator all mean driving on brakes you can't trust.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Photo of dock door 5 with an open trailer and its restraint engaged (indicator showing), a staging lane with stacked pallets, and the neighboring door closed with no trailer. Door numbers repeated as live-text labels. Live-text letter labels A to E (circle shapes, double stroke) sit on the image at each area, matching the options.

blocks.prompt: You're approaching dock door 5 with an empty truck. Select every conflict point.

options.text: Edge of the open trailer
Engaged trailer restraint
Pallet staging lane
Closed neighboring door
Inside the open trailer

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is A, C and E. Drivers step off at the trailer edge, pallets hide people in the staging lane, and workers inside a trailer can be out of sight. An engaged trailer restraint is what you want before entering, and a closed door with no trailer won't put anyone in your path.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is A, C and E. Drivers step off at the trailer edge, pallets hide people in the staging lane, and workers inside a trailer can be out of sight. An engaged trailer restraint is what you want before entering, and a closed door with no trailer won't put anyone in your path.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift at the loading dock.
blocks.description: Operator's view approaching a blind corner beside a dock office door, with a low load.

blocks.prompt: You're carrying a low load toward a blind corner where the dock office door meets the main lane. Which sequence do you run?

options.text: Sound the horn, look, and go through at normal speed if you hear nothing
Slow down, sound the horn, look both ways, yield, make eye contact, proceed
Look both ways, go through, and sound the horn only if you see someone
Slow down, look, and go through; use the horn only if the lane is busy

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: slow down, sound the horn, look both ways, yield, make eye contact, proceed. Slowing first gives you time to react, and the horn is for the people you can't see, so it's used every time, busy lane or not.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: slow down, sound the horn, look both ways, yield, make eye contact, proceed. Slowing first gives you time to react, and the horn is for the people you can't see, so it's used every time, busy lane or not.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest, a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift and a worker in a hi-vis vest on the phone in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's view: a worker in a hi-vis vest steps out between two pallet stacks about 12 feet ahead, turned away and talking to a truck driver.

blocks.prompt: You're crossing the main lane with an empty truck. A temp worker walks out from between two pallet stacks into your lane, talking to a driver, facing away from you. What do you do?

options.text: Sound the horn twice and keep moving at a crawl
Stop, sound the horn and hold until they've seen you and moved clear
Ease around them on the open side of the lane at walking pace
Flash your lights and keep moving slowly so they notice you

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: stop, sound the horn and hold until they've seen you and moved clear. Someone facing away can't make eye contact, and hearing a horn isn't the same as seeing you. Don't keep rolling or steer around them: startled people move unpredictably. Continue only once they're clear.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: stop, sound the horn and hold until they've seen you and moved clear. Someone facing away can't make eye contact, and hearing a horn isn't the same as seeing you. Don't keep rolling or steer around them: startled people move unpredictably. Continue only once they're clear.

pages.title: Question 7: Why a Raised Load Tips

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Side-view diagram of a counterbalance truck with the load raised and the combined CG marker shown high (live-text label 'CG').

blocks.prompt: Why is turning with a raised load more likely to cause a tip-over than turning with the load low?

options.text: Raising the load moves the center of gravity forward, so the truck tips forward in the turn
Raising the load lifts the combined center of gravity, so the turn can push it outside the triangle more easily
Raising the load takes weight off the front wheels, so they lose grip and slide in the turn
Raising the load moves the center of gravity toward the counterweight, so the rear swings out

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: raising the load lifts the combined center of gravity, so the turn can push it outside the triangle more easily. Raising the load doesn't shift the center of gravity forward or back, or change grip at the wheels. The higher it is, the less sideways force it takes to push it past the edge.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: raising the load lifts the combined center of gravity, so the turn can push it outside the triangle more easily. Raising the load doesn't shift the center of gravity forward or back, or change grip at the wheels. The higher it is, the less sideways force it takes to push it past the edge.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of a counterbalance truck in a bulk storage area, forks at head height holding a pallet just lifted off a two-high block stack.

blocks.prompt: You've lifted a pallet off the top of a two-high block stack and backed out just far enough to clear it. The forks are at head height. What next?

options.text: Start toward the dock and lower gradually as you go
Stay stopped, lower to travel height and tilt back, then drive off
Drive at walking pace with it up, since it's a short trip
Keep it up until the turn, then lower before turning

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: stay stopped, lower to travel height and tilt back, then drive off. Raise and lower only when you're stopped, and never travel with the load up, even slowly or for a short trip.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: stay stopped, lower to travel height and tilt back, then drive off. Raise and lower only when you're stopped, and never travel with the load up, even slowly or for a short trip.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Operator's view along aisle 18 toward the aisle end and the main travel lane, with the load carried low.

blocks.prompt: You're carrying a pallet down aisle 18 toward a right turn onto the main travel lane. When should you slow down?

options.text: In the turn, braking as you steer
Before the turn, while you're still traveling straight
After the turn, once you can see the lane
Only if there are pedestrians in the lane

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: before the turn, while you're still traveling straight. Get your speed off on the straight so the turn needs no extra braking. Braking in the turn throws the load forward while the turn pushes it sideways.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: before the turn, while you're still traveling straight. Get your speed off on the straight so the turn needs no extra braking. Braking in the turn throws the load forward while the turn pushes it sideways.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Still: sit-down counterbalance truck mid-turn with the seatbelt visibly unfastened. Non-graphic.

blocks.prompt: On a sit-down counterbalance truck, a turn goes wrong and the truck starts to tip. You realize you didn't fasten your seatbelt. What do you do?

options.text: Jump, since you're not held in anyway
Stay in the seat, grip the wheel, brace your feet and lean away from the fall
Grab the overhead guard with one hand outside the cab
Try to fasten the belt before it goes over

blocks.feedback_correct: The answer is: stay in the seat, grip the wheel, brace your feet and lean away from the fall. Even unbelted, the safest place is inside the overhead guard. Don't jump, don't put a hand outside the cab and don't fumble with the buckle. And always belt up before you move.
blocks.feedback_incorrect: The answer is: stay in the seat, grip the wheel, brace your feet and lean away from the fall. Even unbelted, the safest place is inside the overhead guard. Don't jump, don't put a hand outside the cab and don't fumble with the buckle. And always belt up before you move.

blocks.text: Here's how you did on the assessment.

blocks.alt: Illustration of a worker in a hi-vis vest and a worker in a hard hat driving the forklift in a warehouse aisle.
blocks.description: Photo of an operator at the end of a shift, parking a truck correctly (forks lowered). The three habits as large live text. A button with a document icon for the PDF.

blocks.text:
Your shift, your calls:
- Inspect for real. Tag out what isn't safe.
- Treat every intersection and dock door as if someone's there.
- Carry low. Slow down before you turn.

This course supports, but doesn't replace, your hands-on evaluation.

That's the course. Pin the quick reference on your huddle board, and keep making these calls the way you just did. Remember, this doesn't replace your hands-on evaluation on the truck. Thanks for your time.
